---
title: "SEPIA"
subtitle: "Systematic Evaluation of Pigmentation In Archaic hominins"
---

**SEPIA** — *Systematic Evaluation of Pigmentation In Archaic hominins* — asks what the
genetics of pigmentation (skin, hair, and eye colour) can, and cannot, tell us about
Neanderthals and Denisovans, and how they compare to present-day human variation. The
recurring public question is *"what did archaic humans look like?"* SEPIA asks how much
their ancient DNA can actually answer — and stays explicit about where the data runs out.

## The approach

SEPIA is a **QC-first re-analysis**. It continues the honors thesis **PAINT** (Lily Heald,
2026) but rebuilds the analysis from clearly-traced inputs, because archaic DNA is patchy
and shallow and pigmentation genes don't behave like ancestry markers. Every figure is
regenerated from a documented pipeline so its provenance is auditable, and known analysis
pitfalls — genome-build mismatches, degenerate PCAs, imputation artefacts — are checked
rather than assumed away.

The work runs as a phased plan: trace inputs → one verified genome build → positive
controls → sample QC → the pigmentation analyses → reproducible infrastructure → writing.

- **[Project plan &amp; roadmap](plan/sepia-plan.html)** — the single phased plan (bug fixes, analysis redesign, QC checks Q1–Q10, infrastructure, writing).
- **[Changelog &amp; decision log](plan/changelog.html)** — dated record of what's been done, found, and decided.
- **[All project documents](plan/docs.html)** — data &amp; pipeline record, per-genome provenance &amp; QC, bug-evidence log, rebuild plan.

## Status

- **v1 — honors thesis (PAINT, 2026, Lily Heald).** Framed the feasibility question: how
  complete and deep is archaic sequencing at pigmentation loci, and where do archaic
  samples fall relative to modern humans?
- **In progress — SEPIA.** Rebuilding on clearly-traced data: a completed modern reference
  panel, a harmonised genome build, genotype-likelihood handling for low-coverage genomes,
  a directionality-based pigmentation score, and redone principal-component analyses — plus
  a *Trends in Genetics* review.

## What the work finds (so far)

Archaic sequencing is uneven and often shallow; missing data is non-random (older samples
have more of it); and pigmentation-associated SNPs on their own don't separate populations
the way the whole genome does. Confident, species-wide claims about archaic pigmentation
aren't well supported — the contribution is an honest map of what the genetics does and
doesn't show.

## Data &amp; provenance

- **Simons Genome Diversity Project (SGDP)** — modern human reference genomes.
- **Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology (MPI-EVA)** — archaic Neanderthal/Denisovan genomes.
- **NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog** — pigmentation-associated variants (the 222-SNP panel).
- **NASA Earth Observations** — UV-index climatology.

Per-file provenance — and where the large / cluster-only data live — is documented in
[`data/README.md`](https://github.com/lasisilab/sepia/blob/main/data/README.md); per-genome
sources are in the [provenance tables](plan/papers/REFERENCES.html).
